clue.text: Guinea pig cages with limitless space

indicators.note: to cage something is to hold it inside, so the rodent's name goes round the next piece

parts.note: a cavy is the zoological name for the guinea pig

indicators.note: without its limits, the word with loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A pet guinea pig is kept caged with no room to move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guinea pig' looks like a test subject but is the animal itself, and 'space' at the end is the definition, not part of the cage.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavity is a hollow, an empty space inside something such as a tooth.

clue.text: Girl, left out, needs makeover

annotationWithheld.why: Girl, left out, needs makeover (8): anagram of GIRL NEEDS less L, but 'makeover' is both the anagram indicator and the definition, a word doing two jobs

clue.text: Proceeded carefully, keeping head of organisation in the loop

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so the verb goes round the letter

parts.note: to nose forward is to edge ahead cautiously

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone cautiously advanced while keeping the boss of the organisation informed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the loop' looks like office jargon for being informed, but taken literally it means caught in a noose.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, being in the loop means having a rope's slipknot around the neck.

clue.text: Ruling king's son leaves with child

indicators.note: the prince departs, so his letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: a woman with child is expecting a baby
a king's son is a prince, abbreviated P

explanation.surface: The ruler's son departs, leaving with a child in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with child' looks like the son taking a child along, but it is a synonym for expecting.
explanation.definitionFit: Regnant is a formal adjective for reigning, as in a queen regnant who rules in her own right.

clue.text: The British, perhaps, ponder limits to unilateralism

parts.note: to muse is to think something over

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: The British might well reflect on the boundaries of acting alone in foreign policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The British' looks like the nation; it is the British Museum in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Museum in London is a famous example of an institution displaying historical artefacts.

clue.text: Calls doctor on the spot after tot's scratched

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged
something scratched is withdrawn, as a horse from a race

parts.note: the word tot is struck out of the letters, the possessive adding nothing

explanation.surface: A medic is summoned at once after a toddler gets a scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratched' looks like the child's injury; it says TOT is taken from the letters of ON THE SPOT, and 'doctor' rearranges the remaining ONHESP.
explanation.definitionFit: Phones as a verb means rings up or calls someone on the telephone.

clue.text: Skeleton of English doctor found on far side of watering hole

indicators.note: the pieces sit after the first, beyond it in reading order

parts.note: a watering hole is informal for a pub or bar
Bones is the nickname of the doctor in Star Trek, and slang for any doctor

explanation.surface: An English medic's skeleton is discovered beyond a desert oasis.
explanation.definitionFit: The bare bones of something are its skeleton, the essential framework without detail.

clue.text: Thick, like George?

definitions.meaning: dense and full, as a beard or tail can be
resembling either US president George Bush, a joke on his surname

explanation.definitionFit: Bushy means growing thickly, like a dense hedge or a full head of hair.

clue.text: Dangerous allure of wailing German

parts.note: when sirens are on, they wail, so the phrase describes the noise

explanation.surface: A German's mournful cries hold a perilous attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wailing German' looks like a weeping person; split it as SIRENS ON (the wailing) plus G.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Sirens' singing lured sailors to wreck, so the phrase means any fatally tempting appeal.

clue.text: Crumbling as one ages

indicators.note: something crumbling breaks apart, so the letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Things crumble as one grows older.
explanation.definitionFit: An aeon is an immeasurably long period, so aeons are ages in the loose sense of a very long time.

clue.text: Leading members of judiciary are merciless, but upright

indicators.note: the first letters of the following words lead them

explanation.surface: The senior judges are pitiless, though honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upright' looks like a moral quality of the judges; it is a noun for a vertical post.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamb is the vertical side post of a door or window frame.

clue.text: Many miss working on farm, lacking support in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters read backwards
the word for help is missing from the longer word

parts.note: a dairymaid is a girl who works in a farm's dairy
aid is help or support

explanation.surface: Lots of farm girls have no help once they stop working.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking AID from DAIRYMAID leaves DAIRYM, which 'in retirement' turns back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Myriad means countless or very many, from the Greek for ten thousand.

clue.text: One warm kiss leads to discharge, almost a disaster

indicators.note: the leading letter of each word is let go, removed from the phrase

explanation.surface: A passionate kiss provokes a release, which is nearly calamitous.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first letters O, W, K of One, Warm, Kiss and NE ARM ISS remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A near miss is an incident that very nearly becomes an accident or collision.

clue.text: Blowing top in burning fury

indicators.note: losing its top, the word drops its first letter

parts.note: a burning is a fire

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper in a fit of burning rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowing top' looks like losing one's temper, but it removes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is a literary word for anger or rage.

clue.text: Take action against Twycross, perhaps, after loss of larynx

indicators.note: without the larynx a voiced sound becomes unvoiced, so the word is spoken with a hiss in place of a buzz

parts.note: Twycross Zoo is a zoo in Leicestershire, England

explanation.surface: Someone sues Twycross after losing their voice.
explanation.walkthrough: Z is the voiced partner of S: say ZOO without the voice box's buzz and it comes out as SUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue is to take legal action against someone in court.

clue.text: Idiotic change of heart for woman giving evidence

indicators.note: the central letter of the word is changed for another

parts.note: witless means stupid or idiotic

explanation.surface: A foolish woman alters her testimony.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle L of WITLESS becomes N; the clue does not name the new letter, which the definition and crossings settle.
explanation.definitionFit: A witness is a person giving evidence in court, here pictured as a woman.

clue.text: Later, perhaps, served up dumpling

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the letters rise and read backwards

parts.note: saying later is one way of saying not now

explanation.surface: A dumpling is served up some time afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' looks like dishing out food; in a down entry it turns NOT NOW upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A wonton is a small Chinese dumpling, often served in soup.

clue.text: See 16
In disguise, the Fourth Man

indicators.note: the letters are found in the run of the next words

explanation.surface: A mysterious fourth man appears in disguise, like a spy story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Fourth Man' suggests a spy ring; he is the fourth man of Genesis, after Adam, Cain and Abel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Seth is Adam and Eve's third son, the fourth man after Adam, Cain and Abel.

clue.text: Disgusting smell, revolting sight

indicators.note: to revolt is to turn over, so the letters are turned round

parts.note: BO is body odour, a bad smell
a scene is a view or sight

explanation.surface: A foul odour and a repulsive spectacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' reads as disgusting but turns BO into OB.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscene means offensive and repugnant, especially to moral standards.

clue.text: Reduced speed in Washington DC, perhaps steering clear of Congress

indicators.note: the shortened word goes inside the other

parts.note: Washington DC is an example of a city

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: haste is speed

explanation.surface: Slowing traffic in the US capital, perhaps by avoiding the legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks like the US legislature; it means sexual intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Chastity means abstaining from sexual intercourse, which the clue calls congress.

clue.text: Church accepts favours to provide absolution

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the abbreviation goes round the word

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
to lean towards something is to favour it

explanation.surface: The church takes favours in exchange for forgiveness.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleanse in a religious sense is to purify from sin, as absolution does.

clue.text: For example, H. Mantel on Reformation?

indicators.note: re-forming the letters puts them in a new order

explanation.surface: Novelist Hilary Mantel writing on the Reformation, as in her Tudor novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'H.' looks like Hilary Mantel's initial; it is the chemical symbol for hydrogen.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydrogen, symbol H, is an element classed among those that are not metals.

clue.text: Where anyone can study review of Disney's Robin Hood?

parts.note: the OU, the Open University, admits students without entry qualifications

indicators.note: reviewing is looking back, so the name reads backwards

parts.note: Walt was Disney's first name

explanation.surface: A critic's take on Disney's animated Robin Hood, studied anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is a British distance-learning university open to all.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood is the famous English legendary figure living outside the law in Sherwood Forest.

clue.text: As a rule, alimony's handled badly and lovelessly

indicators.note: something handled badly is mangled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive adding no letter
love is zero in tennis, the letter O, which is left out

explanation.surface: Divorce payments are usually managed poorly and without affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the O (love) from ALIMONY and 'handled badly' rearranges ALIMNY.
explanation.definitionFit: Mainly means for the most part, much as generally or as a rule do.

clue.text: Rush to indict Bill

definitions.meaning: to rush at someone is to attack headlong
to accuse formally of a crime
a bill is the price asked for something

explanation.surface: Someone hurries to accuse a man named Bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Charge means to attack at speed, to accuse formally, and a fee demanded.

clue.text: Curve in road about to get warning sign

parts.note: C is circa, Latin for about
the amber traffic light warns drivers

explanation.surface: A bend in the road is coming up with a caution signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A camber is the slight convex curve across a road surface that drains water.

clue.text: Banks, for instance, operate on the basis of a deception

parts.note: to go is to work or operate, as a machine does
taken as written
a lie is a deception

explanation.surface: Banks operate on the basis of a deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like financial institutions; it is Gordon Banks, England's 1966 World Cup goalkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordon Banks was a famous England goalkeeper, an example of the player guarding the net.

clue.text: Reportedly waited around grave

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the phrase is spoken

parts.note: to wait around is to stay put

explanation.surface: Someone is said to have lingered around a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grave' looks like a burial place; it is the adjective meaning serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Staid means sober, sedate and serious in manner, close to grave.

clue.text: Split personality?

parts.note: a person from Split, the Croatian city on the ... coast

explanation.definitionFit: A native of Split lives in Dalmatia, the coastal region of Croatia, so is from that region.

clue.text: America's wholesale decline

indicators.note: the possessive reads as has, so the bigger word holds the letter

parts.note: buying wholesale is buying in bulk

explanation.surface: The United States experiences a decline in its wholesale trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decline' looks like a noun for a fall; it is the verb meaning refuse.
explanation.definitionFit: To baulk is to refuse or hesitate to go ahead, as a horse refuses a jump.

clue.text: Fix Cartesian coordinates wrongly

indicators.note: to coordinate wrongly is to arrange badly, so the letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A mathematician corrects Cartesian coordinates that were plotted wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cartesian coordinates' looks like a maths phrase; 'coordinates' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascertain is to find out for certain, to fix or establish a fact.
